title: Adaptive Duty-Cycling for TinyML Human Activity Recognition on a Cortex-M3 Microcontroller: A Simulation-Based Energy and Accuracy Evaluation
content: Continuous human activity recognition (HAR) on wearable and edge devices is fundamentally constrained by battery capacity, yet most on-device HAR systems sample and classify at a fixed rate regardless of the wearer’s actual movement state, wasting energy during long periods of inactivity. This paper presents a TinyML HAR system on a resource-constrained STM32F103C8T6 (Arm Cortex-M3) microcontroller with an MPU6050 inertial measurement unit (IMU), coupled with an adaptive duty-cycling scheme that modulates the sampling and inference interval between 150 ms and 3000 ms based on a windowed accelerometer-magnitude-variance feature computed entirely on-device. When the wearer is stationary the system relaxes its sampling interval toward the upper bound, and tightens it toward the lower bound as movement variance increases. A persistent I2C bring-up fault on the physical prototype prevented on-hardware, real-subject data collection within the project timeline (Section IV); the system is therefore characterized instead through (a) an offline simulation that runs the unmodified, deployed classification code against a physically-motivated synthetic gait model, and (b) a first-principles current-draw estimate built from cited component-level current figures rather than an on-device power profile. In this offline evaluation the rule-based classifier reaches 87.0% overall accuracy across three activity classes (100% stationary, 90.2% walking, 70.9% running recall), and the duty-cycling policy is estimated to reduce average current draw by approximately 87% (≈ 7.7×) relative to an always-on fixed-rate baseline built from the same component figures — with a further ≈98% (≈ 56×) reachable once a concrete, identified gap (the IMU is not yet power-cycled between duty-cycle wake events) is closed. These results characterize the system’s design and control logic, not its validated real-world performance; Section VI states plainly what on-hardware validation remains.
